sentences.text:
The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
(Pfa Act), alleging that the accused has violated the provisions of the Pfa Act and Rules.

The
acc
used is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. Guru Masala Stall, from where the food article, that is, 'Lal Mirch Powder' was lifted for sampling.

2. As per the complaint, on 29.01.2011, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) A. K.
Singh and Field Assistant (FA) J. S. Bisht under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. R. K. Sharma reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Guru Masala Stall at Stall No.1, Mirch Masala Market, Pul Bangash, Azad Market, Delhi - 110006, where the accused was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption.
The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Lal Mirch Powder which was being sold in loose condition, from the vendor to which he agreed.
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.
Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.

In Re vs Guru @ Gurusaran on 7 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/40250656/
1 Vide report dated 17.02.2011, the PA found the sample to be conforming to the standards.

However,
as the food article was being sold in loose and unpacked condition in violation of Clause 24 of Rule 49 of PFA Rules, investigation was conducted.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court on 24.03.2011 alleging violation of section 7(v) of PFA Act, as punishable section 16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 24.03.2011.

4. Based on the contents of the complaint, notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC was framed against the accused on 20.09.2011 for commission of the offence punishable under section 16(1)(a)
PFA Act, being violation of section 7(v) of PFA Act, read with Rule 49 (24) of PFA Rules, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
5. At the trial, prosecution examined three witnesses in support of its case.

PW-1 FI A. K. Singh,
PW-2 Sh. R. K. Sharma (SDM/LHA) and PW-3 FA J. S. Bisht were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 29.01.2011 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings,
including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1500 gram of Lal Mirch Powder that was being sold in open and loosed condition,
dividing it in three parts, fastening, sealing, marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex.
PW- 1/A, Notice Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B, Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C, Raid Report Ex.PW-1/D, Statement of accused Ex. PW1/E, PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/F and LHA receipt Ex. PW-1/G. PA report Ex. PW-1/H was received and investigation was conducted by PW-1 who sent letters Ex. PW-1/I to Ex. PW-1/M to various authorities and accused.
He received reply of the accused Ex. PW-1/N.
After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW- 1/O was taken from the Director PFA and thereafter, complaint Ex. PW- 1/P was filed in the court.
A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/Q was sent to the accused through post.
PW-1 and PW-2 were duly cross
- examined by the Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the accused had been falsely implicated or that the accused was packing the Mirch Powder in packets.
PW-3 was however not cross-
examined by the accused despite opportunity.
6. Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 24.02.2016 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Though he admitted the proceedings dated 29.01.2011, yet he claimed that the sample was not in open condition and was in a sealed packet of one kg.
He chose not to lead evidence in defence.

7. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt as all the witnesses have supported its case and no material contradiction can be seen in their testimonies.
In Re vs Guru @ Gurusaran on 7 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/40250656/
2 8.
On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has argued that no case is made out against the accused.
The sole ground urged by the defence is that no public witness was joined in the proceeding to corroborate the version of the official witnesses.
9. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant as well as Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.
10. It is to be understood that the present is not a case of selling any adulterated or misbranded food article.
The PA report Ex. PW-1/H clearly shows that the sample was conforming to the standards and there was no deficiency in its nature, substance or quality.
There is no allegation of any kind of adulteration in the food article on any of the parameters provided under section 2(ia) of the PFA Act.
11. The case of the complainant is based on the allegation that the food article was being sold in loose condition in violation of Rule 49 (24) of PFA Rules.
This provision, which was added in 1994 and amended in 1999, provides that no person shall sell powdered spices and condiments except under packed conditions.
As per the Explanation to this rule, "spices and condiments" means those specified in Appendix - B of PFA Rules.

12. It is not in dispute that the food article i.e. Lal Mirch Powder falls in Item No. A.05.05.01 of Appendix - B of PFA Rules and is a part of "spices and condiments" as standardized under the Rules.
The defence has also not questioned the applicability of Rule 49(24) to the food article in question.
It is nowhere the stand of the accused that the food article was not a standardized spice or condiment or was not in powdered form.
13. The defence has tried to take a stand that the food article was not being actually sold to any customer.

Ld. Counsel has pointed out that as per PW-1, accused was selling the food article to the customers but he stopped upon noticing them, and has thus argued that no such customer has been joined in investigation who could depose and prove the fact that any such product was sold or was meant for sale.
14. However, I do not find force in the said submissions.

It is to be understood that the word "sale"
used in the PFA Act has as wide connotation when compared to its meaning in common parlance.
As per Section 2 (xiii) of PFA Act, "sale" includes even an agreement to sell, offer to sell, exposing for sale, having in possession for sale, attempt to sell and also sale for analysis.
Therefore, it is not necessary that a food article should actually being sold to a customer and that customer be joined to prove such sale, to establish the factum of sale under the PFA Act.
There is no rule that the food officials can lift the sample of only that food article which is being sold to any customer.

Even if there is no customer to whom the product is being sold or any such customer is not joined as a witness, the factum of sale can still be proved under section 2(xiii) of PFA Act.
15.
In the present case, it is not in dispute that the accused was in possession of Lal Mirch Powder which had been exposed for sale for human consumption.
PW-1 also deposed that it was being sold to customers but when the accused noticed them, he stopped selling the same to any customer.

In In Re vs Guru @ Gurusaran on 7 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/40250656/
3 any case, the accused had sold the article to the FI himself for analysis for which payment was also made to him vide Ex.PW1/A, which also would bring the matter within the purview of PFA Act.

Even the accused in his statement under section 313 CrPC accepted such proceedings to be correct,
though claimed that the sample was in sealed condition.
The accused never raised defence at the trial to the effect that the food article was not for sale or was for any purpose other than sale.
16. It is again not in dispute that the accused was the proprietor of the premises / business concern from where the sample was lifted.
He was the vendor from whom the sample was taken.
It is not his case that the sample was not lifted from him or that some other person was responsible for the affairs of the business concern.
17. The fact that the food article was being sold in a loose condition by the accused, has been sought to be proved through the three PWs by the prosecution.
All the three PWs have corroborated the stand of each other on this fact and have stated in one voice that the commodity was lying in loose and open condition.
There is no contradiction in their statements that can be said to be material enough so as to go to the root of the matter.
There is nothing to disbelieve them or to shake their credibility on this point.
The evidence of PW-3 has remained unrebutted.
No suggestion was given to PW-1 or PW-2 to the effect that the food article was lying in sealed or packed condition, as claimed by the accused in his statement under section 313 CrPC.
Rather PW-2 was given suggestion that the accused was packing the food article in packets, which stand was never taken by the accused in his statement.
It is therefore clear that even the stand of the accused is contradictory.
He has not taken a specific stand as to if the food article was lying in sealed / packed condition or if it was yet to be sealed / packed.
In any case, no evidence has been lead by the accused to establish either of the two stands.

There is no witness who could support the accused and depose about the condition in which the food article was lying, in contradiction to what has been proved by the three PWs in corroboration to each other.
There is no material on record to disbelieve the version of the three PWs on this point.

Rather the stand of the accused that the food article was lying in sealed packet of one kg, does appear to be correct, because the FI had lifted the sample of 1500 grams of food article and not that of one kg or any multiple of one kg.
It is nowhere the case of the accused that the FI had opened the sealed packets of one kg each and then divided them in three parts of 500 grams each.
Rather the suggestion put to PW-2 was that the product was being packed by the accused.
Such contradictory stand have weakened the case of the accused.
18. The fate of the case depends on quality of witnesses and not their quantity or designation or professions.
There is no rule of law that requires the evidence of food officials to be viewed with any suspicion.
What is required is that attempt is made to join public persons as witnesses as a matter of prudence.
The court is not oblivious of reluctance of public persons to join such legal proceedings that involves lengthy procedural formalities and strict future commitments.
But non joining of such witnesses would not negate the testimony of official witnesses when they are otherwise truthful and credit worthy and have withstood the test of cross-examination.
No motive has shown to exist giving them reason to depose falsely against the accused.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shriram Labhaya v. MCD [1948-1997 FAC (SC) 483] has categorically held that testimony of the Food Inspector alone,
if believed, is sufficient to convict the accused and there is no requirement of independent corroboration by public persons unless the testimony suffers from fatal inconsistencies.

No such In Re vs Guru @ Gurusaran on 7 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/40250656/
4 inconsistency can be seen in this case.
No violation of any rule or provision has been pointed out by the defence.
19. In view of this discussion, it can be said that the complainant / prosecution has been able to establish its case and prove the guilt of the accused beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.

It has been proved that the accused had sold a powdered spice or condiment in loose / unpacked condition in violation of Rule 49(24) of PFA Rules, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7(v) read with section 16(1)(a) of PFA Act.

Thus, the accused is held guilty and convicted for the offence punishable under section 16(1)(a) of the PFA Act.
20. Let the matter be listed for arguments on sentence.

Announced in the open court this 07st day of November 2016 ASHU GARG ACMM-II (New Delhi),
